claim: For a mobile app, the IAM guide says not to embed access keys in the app, even in encrypted storage, and to use Amazon Cognito to manage user identities and the Cognito credentials provider to manage the credentials the app uses for AWS requests.
question: Where should a mobile app get the AWS credentials it uses, and may access keys be embedded in it?

values.display: Don't embed access keys with the app

evidence.quote: Don't embed access keys with the app, even in encrypted storage. Instead, use [Amazon Cognito](https://aws.amazon.com/cognito/) to manage user identities in your app.
You can then use the Amazon Cognito credentials provider to manage credentials that your app uses to make requests to AWS.

claim: The IAM guide recommends Amazon Cognito whenever possible for mobile and web app federation, because it does most of the work with public identity providers and also supports anonymous sign-ins; working directly with an OIDC-compatible provider is for more advanced scenarios.
question: For a web or mobile app, does AWS recommend calling AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity with a social IdP token directly, or using Amazon Cognito?

qualifiers.scope: federation for mobile and web apps

evidence.quote: Whenever possible, use Amazon Cognito for mobile and web-based application scenarios. Amazon Cognito does most of the behind-the-scenes work with public identity provider services for you. It works with the same third-party services and also supports anonymous sign-ins. However, for more advanced scenarios, you can work directly with a third-party service like Login with Amazon, Facebook, Google, or any IdP that is compatible with OpenID Connect (OIDC).
To use identity federation with Internet identity providers, we recommend you use [Amazon Cognito](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cognito/latest/developerguide/what-is-amazon-cognito.html).
